justification: Finding 0 identifies exactly the defect. The new code reads `handleOrId.refresh` for any non-number return value, and the finding notes that "`isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)` throws a TypeError" when setTimeout and similar calls return null or undefined. This is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: In `patchTimer`'s `scheduleTask`, the change stores the native timer's return value in `handleOrId`. When it is not a number, it executes `data.isRefreshable = isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`. Some environments return null or undefined from `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`requestAnimationFrame`, for example a browser extension, policy or automation wrapper that blocks the call. The old code explicitly tolerated a nullish handle. With this change, reading `.refresh` on null throws a TypeError synchronously, so calling the patched `setTimeout` crashes instead of returning. The fix uses optional chaining (`handleOrId?.refresh`) so a nullish handle is treated as non-refreshable.

justification: The known bug is about newlines inside non-split selector parts being truncated because `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/` uses `.`, which doesn't match newlines. Finding [0] describes a different defect: `slice(prefix.length, -1)` assuming the part ends with `)`, which garbles trailing pseudo-classes. It doesn't mention newlines or the regex's `.`, so it doesn't match.
ground_truth: In `ShadowCss._scopeSelector`/`_applySelectorScope`, the change replaced the simple `/ ?, ?/` comma split and the combinator separator with regexes that do not split inside parentheses. A selector part like `.foo:is(.a,\n.b)` therefore now reaches `_scopeSelectorPart` as a single string that can contain newlines. That function splits the part with `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/`, both in the newly added pseudo-function `:host` branch (`scopedP.match(...)`) and in the non-host branch (`t.match(...)`). Because `.` does not match a newline, everything after the first newline is silently dropped. For example, a component style `.foo:is(.a,\n.b) {}` is emitted as `.foo[contenta]:is(.a,`, with the rest of the selector and the closing parenthesis lost, which breaks the stylesheet. The fix changed the trailing group of both regexes to `([\s\S]*)` so content after newlines is kept.

findings.description: `_pseudoFunctionAwareScopeSelectorPart` assumes any part starting with `:is(` or `:where(` ends with the closing `)`, and does `selectorPart.slice(prefix.length, -1)`. Parts are only split on top-level combinators, so a part like `:is(.a):hover`, `:where(.a).b` or `:is(h1, h2)::before` has trailing text after the paren. The slice then drops the last character of that trailing text instead of the paren. The result is garbled CSS, e.g. `:is(.a):hover` becomes `:is(.a)[contenta]:hove)`. The test for `:where(a):where(b)` only matches because of an odd expected output; that case is broken in the same way.

justification: The only finding is about the missing Bazel load statements in BUILD.bazel. It does not mention the `if (injector)` guard leaving `metadata.dependencies` undefined, nor the frontend template reading `.length` of undefined. It describes an unrelated issue.
ground_truth: In `getLatestComponentState` (component-tree.ts), the change wraps `metadata.dependencies = getDependenciesForDirective(...)` in `if (injector)`. Previously `dependencies` was always assigned on the directive metadata. Now `getInjectorFromElementNode` returns null whenever `ng.getInjector` is not supported (or returns nothing), and in that case `dependencies` is left `undefined`. The DevTools property view template evaluates `controller().directiveMetadata?.dependencies.length > 0`. The optional chain only guards `directiveMetadata`, not `dependencies`. So when an app's global `ng` lacks `getInjector`, selecting a component throws a TypeError reading `length` of undefined and the property panel breaks. The fix guards the template by first checking that `dependencies` exists before reading its `length`.

justification: Finding 1 matches part of the known bug. It says `init()` runs inside the `afterRenderEffect` on every `componentExplorerView` change, so each run "registers another `highlightComponent` listener" and "recreates both tree visualizers." The ground truth names this exact defect, and the fix calls `init()` only once, when the visualizers don't exist yet. Finding 1 does not mention the hidden-tab D3 layout errors, but it identifies the same faulty code and the same re-execution mechanism. Finding 3 notes that the injector tree's visibility workaround was removed, but its stated failure is author `display` styles overriding `[hidden]` so inactive tabs stay visible. ground_truth: This change rewrites `InjectorTreeComponent` to render from an `afterRenderEffect` that runs whenever the `componentExplorerView` input changes. The effect calls `init()` and `updateInjectorTreeVisualization(view.forest)` without checking whether the tab is visible. The change also hides the deferred `ng-injector-tree` with `[hidden]` (display:none) and removes the old `ng-injector- tree.hidden` CSS, which had kept the element laid out with `visibility: hidden`. So once the Injector Tree tab has been opened and the user switches to another tab, every new component explorer view re-runs the effect. D3 then tries to lay out, translate and snap SVG trees inside an element with no layout, which throws errors. `init()` also runs on every effect execution, re-registering the `highlightComponent` listener and recreating the visualizers each time. The fix adds a `hidden` input bound to the host's `[hidden]`, returns early from the effect when it is true (read untracked), and calls `init()` only once, when the visualizers do not exist yet.

findings.description: The new `sortedProviders` computed was added to apply the old sort-by-token behavior, but the template still passes the raw `providers()` input to `<ng-injector-providers>`. Providers are now unsorted, and the sorting that previously happened in the message handler is lost.

`init()` is called inside the `afterRenderEffect` write phase, which reruns whenever `componentExplorerView` changes. Each run registers another `highlightComponent` listener on the message bus, so the listeners accumulate and fire multiple times. Each run also recreates both tree visualizers via `setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer` and `setUpElementInjectorVisualizer`. Zoom and pan state is lost on every view update, and `injectorTreeGraph` and `elementInjectorTreeGraph` are rebuilt every time.

`diDebugAPIsAvailable` is now computed from the latest view only. A view with an empty forest, or one without `resolutionPath`, flips it to false. The `@else` branch then destroys the whole wrapper and its visualizers, and the 'not supported' message shows. Previously the flag stayed true once set. Before the first view arrives, `componentExplorerView` is null, so the 'only available on Angular 17+' message flashes incorrectly.

The `.hidden` class CSS (display:none) was replaced with the `[hidden]` attribute on component host elements. The UA rule `[hidden]{display:none}` is overridden by any author `display` style on the hosts (for example `display:block` or flex). If the hosts set `display`, the inactive tabs would remain visible and overlap the active tab. The injector tree's special visibility workaround was also removed.

justification: Finding 0's second part identifies the known bug: "`get_fields_from_path` is called unguarded and can raise FieldDoesNotExist or NotRelationField for paths that resolve through `getattr` but are not pure field paths. Those columns would crash the changelist instead of rendering." This is the same faulty call and the same mechanism: an uncaught FieldDoesNotExist for method or property paths. The finding's first part describes a different issue, but the second part would lead a maintainer to the actual bug.
ground_truth: The change makes `lookup_field()` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` unconditionally whenever a `list_display` name contains `__`, so it can render boolean icons for related BooleanFields. Before this, such names were resolved only by walking attributes with `getattr`, which also works for paths whose last part is not a concrete model field, such as a method, a property or `__str__` on a related model. `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` for those paths, and the exception is not caught. Because `lookup_field` is shared by the changelist and readonly-field rendering, entries traversing relations, including second-degree ones (e.g. `book__author__get_full_name` or `parent__parent__some_property`), now crash with an exception where they previously displayed fine. The fix removes this lookup from `lookup_field`. It instead resolves the final field only in `items_for_result` when `f` is None, wrapped in `try/except FieldDoesNotExist`.

findings.description: lookup_field now returns the final related field as `f` for any `__` path. `items_for_result` treats a non-None, non-auto_created `f` as a field on the result row itself. If the path ends in a ForeignKey (e.g. `parent__parent`), `f.remote_field` is a ManyToOneRel, so the code runs `getattr(result, f.name)` on the wrong model. The result is either an AttributeError or the wrong object displayed. Before this change `f` was None for these paths, so the value was rendered correctly. Separately, `get_fields_from_path` is called unguarded and can raise FieldDoesNotExist or NotRelationField for paths that resolve through `getattr` but are not pure field paths. Those columns would crash the changelist instead of rendering.

It says this turns lookups that previously returned values into exceptions in the changelist and readonly fields, which is the same defect as the known bug. findings.description: `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)` is called whenever `name` contains `__` and the attribute walk succeeded. The walk uses plain `getattr`, so it succeeds for properties, methods or other non-field attributes on related objects (e.g. `parent__some_property`). In that case `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` or `NotRelationField`, which is not caught. This turns a lookup that used to return a value (changelist and readonly fields) into an exception, a regression for existing users.

`f` is now a real field for related paths, so `items_for_result` takes its `else` branch. If the final field is a ForeignKey (`isinstance(f.remote_field, ManyToOneRel)`), that branch runs `getattr(result, f.name)`. Here `f.name` belongs to the related model, not the row's model, so it raises AttributeError or returns the wrong object for `list_display` entries like `parent__parent`. Previously these rendered the value correctly with `f=None`.

justification: Finding 0 names the same faulty validation path and the same failure mechanism as the choices half of the known bug. It notes that for fields with `choices` the form field is a TypedChoiceField whose "`to_python` only returns a string and does not validate or coerce it." As a result, searching 'foo' against an `IntegerField` with choices reaches the ORM, where "`int('foo')`... raises ValueError and causes a 500 error." The finding does not mention the BooleanField part of the bug, but it identifies a core defect described in the known bug.
ground_truth: The change rewrote `ModelAdmin.get_search_results` so that, for non-text `__exact` search fields, each search term is validated with `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`. Lookups whose term raises `ValidationError` are skipped; all others are passed to the ORM with the converted value. This validation does not reject invalid terms for two kinds of fields. First, fields with `choices` produce a `TypedChoiceField`, whose `to_python()` returns the raw string unchanged. So searching "john" against an `IntegerField(choices=...)` with `field__exact` sends "john" to the ORM, which raises `ValueError` and makes the changelist return HTTP 500. Second, `forms.BooleanField.to_python()` maps almost any non-false string to True, so an arbitrary term like "xyz" against `bool__exact` matches every row where the field is True instead of matching nothing. The fix uses `formfield.clean()` for Typed(Multiple)ChoiceField so values are coerced and validated, and uses strict boolean and null-boolean parsers that raise `ValidationError` for unrecognized strings.

findings.description: Validation relies on `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`, but for fields with `choices` the form field is a TypedChoiceField. Its `to_python` only returns a string and does not validate or coerce it. For example, with an IntegerField that has choices and `search_fields=['status__exact']`, searching for 'foo' passes validation unchanged. The ORM then calls `int('foo')` in `get_prep_value`, which raises ValueError and causes a 500 error. The removed Cast-based code handled this case, so this is a regression. Related: for ForeignKey/relation fields `ModelChoiceField.to_python` runs an extra DB query per search term and returns a model instance.

findings.description: Validation relies on `formfield().to_python()`, which does not validate the type for every field. A non-text field with `choices` (for example an IntegerField) gets a TypedChoiceField. Its `to_python()` only returns `str(value)` and does no coercion or choice check, because coercion happens in `clean()`. A term like 'foo' therefore passes validation and is used in `int_field__exact='foo'`. That raises `ValueError: Field 'x' expected a number` and the changelist crashes with a 500. The removed Cast approach did not crash here.

For ForeignKey exact lookups (such as `author__exact`), `formfield()` returns a ModelChoiceField. Its `to_python()` runs a database query for every search term and every such field. It also applies `limit_choices_to` and the field's queryset, so a term that matches an existing row can be silently dropped. Instantiating the formfield for every term is extra overhead. An empty quoted term (`""`) is converted to None by many formfields, and `exact=None` is then turned into an IS NULL lookup, which changes the meaning of the search.

justification:

ground_truth:
The rewritten `django.utils.text.wrap()` loops over `text.splitlines(True)`, passes each line to `textwrap.TextWrapper.wrap()`, and joins the pieces with "
". `TextWrapper.wrap()` returns an empty list for an empty or whitespace-only line, so those lines vanish from the output. With the default `replace_whitespace=True`, the trailing newline kept by `splitlines(True)` becomes a space and is dropped, so a trailing newline in the input is lost too. For example, `wordwrap("first

second
", 80)` returns "first
second" instead of "first

second
", which merges paragraphs in templates. The fix sets `replace_whitespace=False` and splits with `splitlines()` (no kept ends). It appends the original line whenever the wrapper returns nothing, and appends a final empty element when the text ends with "
".

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It states that `".. in str(filter_expression.var)` is too broad because for constants `FilterExpression.var` is the resolved value, so `{{ "a..b" }}` triggers the warning. It also notes the future error would reject valid templates. Its suggested fix is to check only Variable lookups and inspect `var.var`, which matches the actual fix.
ground_truth: The new deprecation check in `Parser.parse()` for variable nodes tests `".." in str(filter_expression.var)`. For constant expressions, `filter_expression.var` is the resolved literal value (a string or translated string), not a `Variable` lookup. So a template containing a literal with two consecutive dots, such as `{{ "a..b" }}` or `{{ 'a..b'|upper }}`, wrongly emits a `RemovedInDjango70Warning` about double-dot lookups. justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It points to ColPairs using `queryset.model._meta.db_table` as the alias in the prefetch filter. It also notes that the old name-based `__in` filter resolved this correctly. ground_truth: `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.get_prefetch_querysets()` now filters with `TupleIn(ColPairs(queryset.model._meta.db_table, related_fields, related_fields, self.field), ...)`, where `related_fields = self.field.foreign_related_fields`. Those are fields of the FK's target model, but the table alias comes from the prefetch queryset's model. With a custom prefetch queryset on a multi-table- inheritance subclass of the target, the two do not match. Example: a FK to `Place` prefetched with `Prefetch("place", queryset=Restaurant.objects.all())`. The generated SQL references the parent's column (e.g. `id`) on the child's table, which has no such column, so `prefetch_related` crashes with a database error. The old `field__in` kwarg filter resolved the field names through the ORM and did not have this problem. The fix resolves each field by name against the prefetch queryset (`queryset.query.resolve_ref(field.name).target`), so the columns match the queryset's model.

findings.description: The prefetch filter now builds ColPairs with `queryset.model._meta.db_table` as the alias, for every forward FK including single-column ones. If the target field is defined on a parent model (multi-table inheritance, or a `to_field` inherited from a parent), its column lives in the parent's table, not the child's. justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says that `writer="html"` passes a string where docutils before 0.22 expects a Writer instance. justification: Finding 0 flags the root defect in the bug: "The new <button> elements are created without type=\"button\", so they default to type=\"submit\" inside the admin form." It frames the consequence differently (paths that bypass preventDefault could submit the form) rather than Enter-key implicit submission firing the selector button's handler. Still, it is the same faulty code with the same fix of adding type="button", and it would lead a maintainer to the real bug. Finding 1 concerns aria-label on help icons, which is unrelated.
ground_truth: In `SelectFilter.init` in SelectFilter2.js, the change replaced the "Choose all", "Choose selected", "Remove selected" and "Remove all" `<a>` links with `<button>` elements built via `quickElement('button', ...)`. None of them is given a `type` attribute. Inside a form, a button with no type defaults to `type="submit"`. When a user presses Enter in a text input of an admin change form containing a filter_horizontal/filter_vertical widget, the browser's implicit submission activates the first submit button in tree order. If one of these selector buttons comes first, its click handler fires (moving options, with the event default prevented) instead of the form being saved. The fix adds `'type', 'button'` to all four buttons so they no longer act as submit buttons.

findings.description: The new <button> elements are created without type="button", so they default to type="submit" inside the admin form. Their only protection against submitting the form is e.preventDefault() in the click handlers. justification: Finding [1] identifies the same defect: "The field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields... ground_truth: The new `Index.check()` method passes `{*self.fields, *self.include, *references}` to `model._check_local_fields()`. `self.fields` holds the raw field strings, including the "-" prefix used for descending order. The old Model-level check used the field names from `index.fields_orders`, which has that prefix stripped. As a result, a valid index such as `models.Index(fields=["-name"], name="idx")` now fails the system check with "'indexes' refers to the nonexistent field '-name'" (models.E012). The fix passes `field for field, _ in self.fields_orders` instead of `self.fields`.

findings.description: The database-feature warnings (W037, W040, W043) scan all of `model._meta.indexes` via `any(... for index in model._meta.indexes)`, and the W037 test even uses `self.condition` inside the generator. `Index.check()` now runs once per index, so each of these warnings is emitted once per index in the model whenever any index triggers it. justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says `relatedWindows` is local and not on `window`, so `window.relatedWindows` is undefined in production. justification: Finding [0] is about expression-valued fields being appended twice to returning_fields, which produces duplicate RETURNING columns. The known bug is a different defect: non-expression db_returning fields are removed from returning_fields even on backends that support RETURNING, so the instance keeps stale in-memory values. The finding does not identify that removal mechanism.
ground_truth: In the insert branch of `Model._save_table`, the change builds `returning_fields = list(meta.db_returning_fields)` and then, for each insert field, calls `returning_fields.remove(field)` (the `elif field.db_returning:` branch) whenever the field's pre_save value is not an expression. Before this change, every `db_returning` field was always fetched back via RETURNING and assigned to the instance. Now a `db_returning` field with an explicitly set value keeps the in-memory Python value instead of the value the database actually stored. This happens even on backends that support RETURNING (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle). For example, an explicitly set primary key or a custom `db_returning=True` field whose stored or converted value (via `from_db_value`, normalization or triggers) differs from the assigned value is left stale on the instance after `save()`/`create()`. The fix only removes such fields from `returning_fields` when the backend cannot return columns from insert, and never removes the auto field when the pk was set.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It notes that the new ValueError is raised for over-long codes, that callers "only catch LookupError", and that get_language_from_path() and the cookie path in get_language_from_request() can therefore crash with "an unhandled ValueError (HTTP 500)". This is exactly the known bug's mechanism and symptom.
ground_truth: The security patch added a length check to `get_supported_language_variant()`. When `lang_code` exceeds `LANGUAGE_CODE_MAX_LENGTH` (500) and no generic variant can be cut off (or `strict=True`), it raises `ValueError("'lang_code' exceeds the maximum accepted length")`. So a request whose URL language prefix or language cookie is longer than 500 characters crashes with an unhandled ValueError (HTTP 500) instead of falling back to another language. Fixed by raising `LookupError(lang_code)` instead of ValueError.

justification: The known bug is that casting to a parameterized type such as `varchar(50)[]` or `numeric(5,2)[]` silently truncates or rounds values. Finding 0 also concerns the cast type taken from `db_type()`, but its mechanism is different: "pseudo-types such as `serial`" being rejected. It never mentions truncation or rounding caused by length or precision parameters. Finding 1 is about custom placeholders being ignored, which is unrelated. Neither finding matches.
ground_truth: The new `SQLInsertCompiler.assemble_as_sql` in the PostgreSQL compiler builds each UNNEST placeholder as `(%s)::<db_type>[]`, where `db_type` comes from `field.db_type(self.connection)`. That type string includes the column's parameters, e.g. `varchar(50)` or `numeric(5, 2)`. In PostgreSQL an explicit cast to a length- limited type silently truncates or rounds values instead of raising an error. So `bulk_create()` of two or more objects whose CharField value exceeds `max_length` silently inserts a truncated string, where the regular VALUES insert would fail with a "value too long" error. The same applies to rounding of decimals. The fix strips the parameters from the type (`db_type.split("(")[0]`), so the cast is to e.g. `varchar[]` and the column's own constraints apply on insert.

findings.description: The cast type comes from `field.db_type()`, which returns pseudo-types such as `serial`, `bigserial` and `smallserial` for AutoField, BigAutoField and SmallAutoField. A bulk_create with explicit primary keys on such a field, or on a FK-less model with an auto pk set, generates `(%s)::serial[]`. PostgreSQL rejects this because `serial` is not a real type. `cast_db_type()` should be used instead, since it maps these fields to real types such as `integer`.

The UNNEST path ignores per-field `get_placeholder()` and any placeholder customisation that the base `assemble_as_sql` applies. Fields with custom placeholders, such as geometry fields or user-defined fields, are cast with a plain `(%s)::type[]` and so lose their wrapping SQL. The eligibility check never excludes such fields, so they get wrong SQL or a wrong result.

Other fields whose prepared values or placeholders are not plain literals are affected the same way.

justification: The known bug is a pickling failure: the namedtuple's type name "Attachment" does not match its module attribute name `EmailAttachment`. Finding [0] describes a different issue. It covers backward compatibility when plain tuples are appended to `alternatives` ("now raises AttributeError when `message()` is called"). It says nothing about the naming mismatch or about pickling.
ground_truth: The change adds the module-level `EmailAttachment = namedtuple("Attachment", ["filename", "content", "mimetype"])` in `django/core/mail/message.py`. `EmailMessage.attach()` now stores each attachment as an instance of it. Pickle serializes namedtuple instances by looking up the class by its `__qualname__` ("Attachment") in its module. No `Attachment` attribute exists in `django.core.mail.message`; the class is bound to the name `EmailAttachment`. As a result, pickling an `EmailMessage` with any attachment fails with a `PicklingError` (attribute lookup Attachment on django.core.mail.message failed), e.g. `msg.attach("a.txt", "x", "text/plain"); pickle.dumps(msg)`, which breaks queuing emails through task queues or caches. The fix renames the namedtuple type names to match their variable names (`namedtuple("EmailAttachment", ...)`, and likewise `EmailAlternative`).

findings.description: _create_alternatives now reads `alternative.content` and `alternative.mimetype`, so it only works with Alternative namedtuples. Existing code that appends plain `(content, mimetype)` tuples to `msg.alternatives`, or assigns a list of plain tuples after construction, used to work and now raises AttributeError when `message()` is called. Only `__init__` and `attach_alternative` convert to the namedtuple. This breaks backward compatibility, even though the new docs say alternatives should only be added through `attach_alternative`.

justification: Finding 0 describes the right mechanism: under multi-table inheritance, a child's `pk_fields` holds only the parent link, so the parent's `id` is not excluded. However, it applies this to a different piece of code. It flags `bulk_update` in query.py ("`bulk_update(objs, ['id'])` on a child model is no longer rejected"). The known bug is the `Options._non_pk_concrete_field_names` change in options.py, which affects the `save(update_fields=...)` validation and the `update_or_create` update_fields check. Since the faulty code differs, this does not match under the strict criteria.
ground_truth: The change rewrote `Options._non_pk_concrete_field_names` in options.py to filter with `if field not in self.pk_fields` instead of `if not field.primary_key`. Under multi-table inheritance, a child model's `pk_fields` contains only its own primary key (the parent link). The parent's primary key (e.g. the parent's `id` AutoField) also appears in the child's `concrete_fields` with `primary_key=True`, but it is not in the child's `pk_fields`. As a result, the parent's pk is now reported as an updatable non-pk concrete field. For example, `child.save(update_fields=["id"])` no longer raises the expected ValueError, and code relying on this set, such as the `update_or_create` update_fields subset check, treats the parent pk as a regular field. The fix collects the `pk_fields` of the model and of all its parents (`all_parents`) and excludes all of them. It also updates the save() error message to mention primary keys.

findings.description: The check changed from `f.primary_key` to `f in self.model._meta.pk_fields`. With multi-table inheritance, a child model's `pk_fields` is the parent link field, not the parent's `id`. `bulk_update(objs, ['id'])` on a child model is no longer rejected, even though `id` is a primary key field and was rejected before. This is a likely regression for inherited models.

justification: Finding [0] describes a TypeError arising when max_length=None is compared with an int in the form field. The known bug, by contrast, is a TypeError from calling len() on non-string inputs, such as IPv6Address instances or ints, in is_valid_ipv6_address. ground_truth: The change makes `is_valid_ipv6_address()` call the new helper `_ipv6_address_from_str()` instead of `ipaddress.IPv6Address(ip_str)`. The helper begins with `if len(ip_str) > max_length`, and `is_valid_ipv6_address()` still only catches `ValueError`. Before, non-string values that `ipaddress.IPv6Address` accepts, such as an `ipaddress.IPv6Address` instance or an int, were handled. Now they raise an uncaught `TypeError` (e.g. "object of type 'IPv6Address' has no len()"). justification: Finding 0 points at the faulty guard: it "checks `currentSelect.id` instead of the target `select.id`". It explains that `add_to_cache(select.id, option)` then runs on plain FK selects that have no cache entry, which "throws a TypeError, because `cache[id]` is undefined". That is the same defect and mechanism as the known bug. The fix of adding a `SelectBox.cache[select.id]` check follows directly from this finding.
ground_truth: The change added a block to `updateRelatedSelectsOptions` in RelatedObjectLookups.js that, after appending a new option to another related select, calls `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` and `SelectBox.redisplay(select.id)`. The guard is only `window.SelectBox !== undefined && !SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]`; it never checks that `select` itself is managed by SelectBox. Consider a form with several relations to the same model where only some use `filter_horizontal`, so SelectBox.js is loaded. Adding an object via the '+' popup then reaches other plain `<select>` widgets that have no `SelectBox.cache` entry. `add_to_cache` then pushes onto an undefined cache entry and throws a TypeError. That aborts `dismissAddRelatedObjectPopup`, so the popup window never closes. The fix adds the condition `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`, so the cache is updated only for fields SelectBox actually manages.

findings.description: The SelectBox cache guard checks `currentSelect.id` instead of the target `select.id`. If the page loads SelectBox.js and the current select is a plain FK select with no cache entry, the condition is true for every other related select. `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` then runs against selects that may also have no cache entry, such as another plain FK select. That throws a TypeError, because `cache[id]` is undefined, and aborts the update loop. In the opposite case, where the current select is a filter box with a cache entry (the m2m popup path), the guard is false, so other filter-widget selects for the same model never get their cache updated and the new option can vanish on the next redisplay or filter.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It names the same faulty code: get_error_message() "applies `% self.min_length` to the ngettext msgids before the translation lookup". It gives the same mechanism, that the msgids "no longer match any entry in the locale files". It gives the same symptom, that the error is "always shown in English". It also notes the dropped params, which the fix restores.
ground_truth: The new `MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message()` applies `% self.min_length` to each string literal before passing it to `ngettext`. The msgids that `ngettext` receives are therefore already formatted strings, such as "This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters.". These never match the translation catalog entries, which contain the `%d` placeholder. As a result, with a non-English active language (e.g. French), the too-short password error is always shown untranslated in English. The fix calls `ngettext` with the unformatted singular/plural msgids and applies `% self.min_length` to the translated result. It also restores `params={"min_length": ...}` on the raised `ValidationError`.

findings.description: MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message() applies `% self.min_length` to the ngettext msgids before the translation lookup. The msgids are now "...at least 8 character." instead of the catalog's "...at least %(min_length)d character.", so they no longer match any entry in the locale files. The "too short" error is therefore always shown in English, a regression for every non-English locale. The change also drops `params={"min_length": ...}` from the ValidationError, so code that reads `error.params` loses that data. Custom overrides also cannot use %(min_length)d placeholders, unlike the similarity validator's %(verbose_name)s.

justification: Finding 2 identifies the same defect. It says the `db` alias is only used for the atomic block, and that the ContentType and Permission queries lack `.using(db)`. As a result, they hit the router-chosen or default database instead of the one being migrated. Findings 0 and 1 describe different issues: icontains matching and the handling of custom permissions.
ground_truth: In the new `RenamePermission._rename`, the code reads `db = schema_editor.connection.alias` but never applies it to the lookups. `ContentType.objects.filter(...)` and `Permission.objects.filter(content_type_id__in=...)` therefore run against the default (router-chosen) database rather than the one being migrated. Running `migrate --database=other` on an app with a `RenameModel` reads and renames permissions in the default database, or finds nothing there. Meanwhile the permissions in the database actually being migrated keep their old codenames and names. The fix adds `.using(db)` to both the ContentType and Permission querysets so the operation works on the migration's database connection.

findings.description: The ContentType lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()` instead of an exact match. Renaming a model such as `User` or `Group` also matches content types like `superuser` or `usergroup` in the same app. The code then rewrites those unrelated models' permission codenames and names to `<prefix>_<newmodel>`, corrupting their permissions or colliding with them. It should filter on `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is renamed, using `codename.split('_')[0]` as the prefix. Custom permissions are therefore rewritten wrongly. For example, `publish_oldmodel` becomes `publish_newmodel` with a generated name, and a codename like `can_publish_article` becomes `can_newmodel`. Several custom permissions can collapse into one, or conflict with the default ones and be silently skipped by the IntegrityError handler. Only the default add/change/delete/view permissions should be renamed.

The `db` alias is only used for the atomic block. `ContentType.objects` and `Permission.objects` queries, and `permission.save()`, do not use `.using(db)` or `using=db`. When migrating a non-default database, the rename reads and writes whichever database the router picks, usually default, instead of the one being migrated. Permissions may then not be renamed on the target database, or be modified on the wrong one.

findings.description: The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, which is a substring match. Renaming `Book` to `Novel` also matches the content types for `BookReview` and `Bookmark` in the same app. Their permissions are then rewritten to `add_novel`, `change_novel`, and so on. Those renames either collide and are silently swallowed by the `IntegrityError` handler, or corrupt unrelated permissions. The lookup should be an exact match on `model=old_model.lower()`.

The prefix is taken as `codename.split("_")[0]` and every permission is renamed to `f"{prefix}_{new_model}"`. The name is also overwritten with `Can {prefix} {verbose}`. Custom permissions such as `can_publish_oldmodel` or `publish_oldmodel` get mangled to `can_newmodel` or `publish_newmodel`, with names like 'Can can new model'. Several different custom permissions on one model collapse onto the same codename and conflict. Custom permission names and codenames that don't follow the default pattern are lost. The new name also ignores any custom `verbose_name` the model defines.

The queries ignore the migration's database alias. `ContentType.objects` and `Permission.objects` go through the default router rather than `.using(db)`. Under multi-database setups, `migrate --database=other` reads and saves permissions on the wrong database. The `db` variable is only used for the atomic block.

The permission rename depends on the content type still having the old model name, but ordering is not guaranteed relative to contenttypes' own `RenameContentType` operation. Both pre_migrate handlers insert directly after `RenameModel`. With the default INSTALLED_APPS order (auth before contenttypes), the contenttypes operation is inserted later at the same index and therefore runs first. The content type is then already renamed, so the lookup by the old model name matches nothing and no permissions are renamed. The tests only pass because they list contenttypes first in `available_apps`.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect: the MRO walk "never tracks names that a subclass has already overridden". As a result, a parent's property that is shadowed by a field or plain attribute in a child "is still reported as a property". It names the same consumers (Model.__init__, get_or_create/update_or_create) and the same fix, a `seen` set.
ground_truth: The rewritten `Options._property_names` iterates over `self.model.__mro__` and adds every name whose value in some `klass.__dict__` is a `property`. It does not check whether a class earlier in the MRO already shadows that name with a non-property attribute. Example: an abstract parent model defines `foo` as a `@property` and a child model overrides `foo` with a plain attribute or a field. `foo` is still reported in the child's `_property_names`. Code that relies on this set then treats the name as a property and mishandles it, for example `Model.__init__`/`_prepare_related_fields` kwargs handling and `QuerySet` create/update_or_create validation. The old `inspect.getattr_static` version resolved the attribute as normal lookup would. The fix tracks names already seen in earlier MRO classes and only counts a property if its name was not defined in a more-derived class.

findings.description: The MRO walk collects every property found in any class's __dict__ and never tracks names that a subclass has already overridden. The old code used inspect.getattr_static, which only looked at the most-derived definition. If a parent defines `foo = property(...)` and a subclass overrides it with a non-property (a model field, a plain attribute or None), `foo` is still reported as a property. `_property_names` is used in Model.__init__ for kwargs handling and in the get_or_create/update_or_create checks, so this can produce wrong results. Examples are a field kwarg being treated as a property setter, or valid defaults being rejected. A `seen` set of names from more-derived classes is needed so only the effective attribute is considered.

justification: Finding [1] describes the same defect. It quotes "`self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` uses Field equality, which is based on creation_counter and model" and says that because of this the query is wrapped in an ExpressionWrapper, so `isinstance(rhs, Query)` is False and the tuple_lookups check is skipped. It also recommends comparing by field type, which is the actual fix. Finding [0] is about FieldError not being caught, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: The new `Subquery.resolve_expression()` is meant to drop the Subquery shim and return the bare resolved `Query`. It is supposed to wrap the query in an `ExpressionWrapper` only when the user passed an `output_field` that differs from the query's own. It tests this with `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field`, but `Field.__eq__` compares fields by `creation_counter` and model, not by kind. So a separately instantiated field such as `IntegerField()` never equals the query's model field. As a result, any `Subquery(..., output_field=X())` is always wrapped in an `ExpressionWrapper`, even when `X` is the same field type as the selected column. Lookups that introspect the right-hand side as a `Query` then no longer recognize it, defeating the purpose of the change. One example is the tuple lookups' `isinstance(self.rhs, Query)` check, which is supposed to raise `NotSupportedError` for composite-pk comparisons against subqueries. The fix compares field types (`type(self.output_field) is not type(resolved.query.output_field)`) instead of using field equality.

findings.description: Subquery.resolve_expression only catches AttributeError around `self.output_field`. When the query's output field cannot be determined, for example a multi-column `values()` such as `values('tenant_id','id')` used against a composite pk, `BaseExpression.output_field` raises FieldError. That error now escapes at resolve time, even though the old code only resolved the output field lazily when it was needed. A tuple lookup against a multi-column Subquery can therefore crash. The except clause should catch FieldError, or use `_output_field_or_none`.

The comparison `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` uses Field equality, which is based on creation_counter and model. An explicitly passed output_field is therefore almost always unequal to the query's own field, even when both have the same type. In that case the resolved query is wrapped in an ExpressionWrapper. The wrapper hides the Query from the right-hand-side introspection that the shim removal was meant to enable, because `isinstance(rhs, Query)` is False. Tuple lookups with an explicit output_field then take the wrong path, and the unsupported-backend check in tuple_lookups.py is skipped. The comparison should be by field type, not instance equality.
